source: Constructed document — based on AP Physics 1 / IB Physics curriculum
notes: Constructed Class C document (25 units, 9 ECUs, nesting depth 3, max orbit 2). Covers horizontal/vertical component decomposition, equations of motion for each axis, range/time-of-flight formulas, symmetry of trajectory, two worked examples (horizontal launch and angled launch), real-world applications (basketball, artillery), video, and a rich exercise set. Multiple multinuclear Sequence relations for stepwise derivations.

units.label: Title: Projectile Motion
units.content_summary: Lesson title

units.label: Hook: basketball free throw (video)
units.content_summary: Slow-motion video of a basketball free throw showing the parabolic arc. Trajectory path traced in red. Question: 'What determines whether the ball goes in?' Sets up the need for projectile motion analysis.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: decompose projectile motion into independent horizontal and vertical components; apply kinematic equations to each axis; calculate range, max height, and time of flight; analyse the effect of launch angle on range.

units.label: Key concept: independence of components (text)
units.content_summary: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontal: constant velocity (no air resistance), ax=0, x=v₀cosθ·t. Vertical: constant acceleration due to gravity, ay=-g=-9.8m/s², vy=v₀sinθ-gt. A bullet fired horizontally hits the ground at the same time as one dropped from the same height — they share the same vertical motion.

units.label: Component independence diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Strobe-light diagram showing a ball thrown horizontally (projectile) alongside a ball dropped vertically. Horizontal positions are equally spaced (constant vx). Vertical positions match exactly (same ay). Proves independence of components.

units.label: Vector decomposition diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Diagram of initial velocity vector v₀ at angle θ to horizontal, decomposed into vx=v₀cosθ (horizontal component) and vy=v₀sinθ (vertical component). Trigonometry labels shown. Right triangle formed by components and resultant.

units.label: Horizontal motion equations (text)
units.content_summary: Horizontal (x-axis): ax=0 (no horizontal force, ignoring air resistance). vx = v₀cosθ = constant (unchanged throughout flight). x = vx·t = v₀cosθ·t. Horizontal motion is uniform — object moves equal distances in equal time intervals.

units.label: Vertical motion equations (text)
units.content_summary: Vertical (y-axis): ay = -g = -9.8 m/s². vy = v₀sinθ - gt. y = v₀sinθ·t - ½gt². At maximum height: vy=0 → t_top = v₀sinθ/g. Max height: H = (v₀sinθ)²/(2g). Vertical motion is uniformly accelerated.

units.label: Equations summary table (image)
units.content_summary: Two-column table: Horizontal | Vertical. Rows: Initial velocity (vx=v₀cosθ | vy₀=v₀sinθ), Acceleration (ax=0 | ay=-g), Velocity at time t (vx=const | vy=v₀sinθ-gt), Position at time t (x=vxt | y=v₀sinθ·t-½gt²). Compact reference.

units.label: Trajectory equation derivation (text)
units.content_summary: Eliminate t between x and y equations: t=x/vx; substitute: y = tanθ·x - gx²/(2v₀²cos²θ). This is the trajectory equation — parabola in the form y = ax - bx². Confirms that projectile paths are parabolic. Symmetry: the descent mirrors the ascent.

units.label: Parabolic trajectory diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Graph showing parabolic trajectory with key points labeled: launch point (0,0), maximum height H at x=R/2, landing point (R,0). Symmetry axis shown at x=R/2. Angle of launch and landing marked as equal (45° case shown). Range R labeled.

units.label: Range formula and optimum angle (text)
units.content_summary: Total time of flight: T = 2v₀sinθ/g. Horizontal range: R = v₀cosθ·T = v₀²sin2θ/g. Maximum range occurs when sin2θ=1 → 2θ=90° → θ=45°. Complementary angles give same range: θ=30° and θ=60° both give R=v₀²sin60°/g. Important result for targeting problems.

units.label: Range vs angle graph (image)
units.content_summary: Graph of range R vs launch angle θ from 0° to 90°. Symmetric curve peaking at θ=45°. Points at 30° and 60° are marked, showing they give identical R values. Confirms the complementary angle theorem.

units.label: Worked Example 1: horizontal launch from cliff (text)
units.content_summary: Problem: ball launched horizontally at 20 m/s from cliff 45m high. Find: (a) time to hit ground, (b) horizontal distance, (c) speed at impact. Solution: (a) 45=½(9.8)t² → t=3.03s; (b) x=20×3.03=60.6m; (c) vx=20, vy=9.8×3.03=29.7; v=√(400+882)=35.8m/s. All steps shown.

units.label: Worked Example 1 trajectory diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Scale diagram of cliff (45m) with parabolic trajectory curving down to landing point 60.6m from cliff base. Velocity vectors shown at three points: launch (horizontal), midpoint (diagonal), impact (steep diagonal). All values labeled.

units.label: Worked Example 2: angled launch (text)
units.content_summary: Problem: ball launched at 30 m/s at 40° above horizontal from ground. Find: (a) max height, (b) time of flight, (c) range. Solution: vx=30cos40°=23.0, vy₀=30sin40°=19.3; (a) H=vy₀²/(2g)=19.0m; (b) T=2×19.3/9.8=3.94s; (c) R=23.0×3.94=90.6m. Full working.

units.label: Worked Example 2 full trajectory diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Annotated parabola for Example 2: shows max height H=19.0m at midpoint, range R=90.6m, launch angle 40°. Horizontal and vertical velocity components shown as arrows at multiple points along trajectory.

units.label: Symmetry of projectile motion (text)
units.content_summary: The trajectory is symmetric about the maximum height. Time to reach max height = time to fall from max height. Speed at launch equals speed at landing (same height). The angle below horizontal at landing equals the launch angle. Useful for simplifying calculations.

units.label: Real-world: basketball shot analysis (text)
units.content_summary: For a free throw: rim is at 3.05m, launch height ~2.0m, horizontal distance ~4.6m. Net height gain = 1.05m. At 45° launch angle: required v₀ ≈ 7.0m/s. However, a slightly steeper angle (52°) gives a wider entry window into the rim. Explains why basketball coaches say 'shoot with arc.'

units.label: Real-world: artillery and air resistance (text)
units.content_summary: Artillery shells follow projectile paths but air resistance reduces range significantly — actual optimum angle is less than 45° (≈38° for typical artillery). Long-range missiles must account for Earth's curvature. Real-world projectiles deviate from ideal parabola at high speeds/distances.

units.label: Air resistance effect diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Overlay of two trajectories at 45°: ideal parabola (blue, no air resistance) vs realistic trajectory (red, with air resistance). Realistic trajectory is shorter, asymmetric (steeper descent than ascent), and peak is shifted left.

units.label: Video: projectile motion simulation (video)
units.content_summary: PhET simulation video showing a projectile launcher at variable angles and speeds. Student adjusts angle from 0° to 90° and observes range changes, confirming the 45° maximum and complementary angle result. Can toggle air resistance on/off.

units.label: Practice problems: basic calculations (text)
units.content_summary: Four basic problems: horizontal launch from height; angled launch finding max height; find angle given range and initial speed; find initial speed given range and angle. Each requires setting up equations from scratch.

units.label: Practice problems: multi-step challenge (text)
units.content_summary: Two challenge problems: (1) Two projectiles launched simultaneously from the same point at different angles — do they ever meet? (2) A ball is kicked toward a wall 10m away at v₀=15 m/s, θ=35°. At what height does it hit the wall? Requires multiple kinematic equations.
